title: Krishna washes the guests' feet
hookLine: jobs are handed out for a king's great sacrifice, and the guest of honor takes the one at the guests' feet
carry: in seva, God takes the job at the feet
tomorrow: a sage sent to learn from a merchant
last: THE SAME HONOR FOR EVERY GUEST.

cards: A great royal sacrifice is underway, and someone has to hand out the jobs. King Yudhishthira is holding the Rajasuya, the rite that marks a king as sovereign, and kings and sages have come from everywhere.
There are crowds to feed, gifts to give, money to guard, elders to look after. So everyone pitches in, the way families do before a big wedding.
And Krishna, the guest this same story has the assembly honor first, has a job too. The Bhagavata's tenth book tells you which one, almost in passing.

teach.b: Here's the Bhagavata's list. Bhima ran the kitchen. Duryodhana kept the treasury.
Sahadeva received the guests, Nakula gathered supplies, and Arjuna looked after the elders. Draupadi served the food. Karna handed out the gifts.
And Krishna washed the feet of the guests. In this same story, the assembly gives Krishna the first honor of the whole ceremony. For his devotees, he is God.

And his job is at the guests' feet, with water, washing off the dust of the road. Water for a guest's feet is part of the traditional Hindu welcome, the same welcome still offered to the deity in daily puja.
Yesterday the guest was God. Here God serves the guests. It's also work done kneeling.
He does it anyway, and the text mentions it in passing, inside a list, as though nothing could be more natural. For a vocation of seva, that short list does two things.

It shows that every job at the feast was service: the treasury and the kitchen, the gifts and the plates. Nobody on that list was there just to be seen. And it shows that the job doesn't measure the person.

teach.h: HONORED FIRST, KNEELING AT THEIR FEET.
teach.b: The one honored first worked at the feet.

teach.h: THE JOB DOESN'T MEASURE THE PERSON.
teach.b: On an ordinary Tuesday, the trash bags and the folding chairs aren't lesser roles in this picture. In the Bhagavata, that's where Krishna stands.

how: At Hindu temple festivals and family ceremonies, volunteers take on the cooking, serving, cleaning and welcoming as seva, and stories like Krishna washing guests' feet at the Rajasuya are told to honor that work.

o: the honor of being the first guest served
service for life, where no job is beneath you
a job handed out at a royal sacrifice

games.q: jobs at the Rajasuya — tap the pairs.

s: at the Rajasuya, Krishna took the seat of honor and did no work
honored first by the assembly, he washed the guests' feet.
in the Bhagavata's list, Duryodhana kept the treasury
the work was split: kitchen, treasury, guests, supplies, elders, food, gifts, feet.
the text makes a long speech about Krishna's humility here
it mentions his job in passing, inside a list of duties.

games.q: you're Krishna at Yudhishthira's great sacrifice. the assembly has just honored you first. jobs are being handed out. which do you take?
games.why: Krishna washes the guests' feet. the one honored first takes the job at their feet, and the text reports it in passing.

practice: Think of a place you'll be this week where things need doing, home, work, a temple, a family gathering, and notice the job you'd hope someone else takes. Picture yourself doing that one gladly, with nobody noticing.
If you pray, you can offer that unchosen work to the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Seva as vocation. Service as a life's work: at Yudhishthira's sacrifice every job is service, and the guest of honor washes feet.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the royal consecration rite that marks a king as sovereign; Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the setting.

carryVoice: Your line: in seva, God takes the job at the feet. The lowest job at the feast went to the one honored first. That's today, done.
